sustainable-innovation/00-concept-sustai: Idée centrale Sustainable innovation does not replace the general logic of innovation: it expands it and adds complexity (new types of value, externalities, a wider value system, a wider scope of analysis). 01 Définition Sustainable innovation General definition (course) The intentional introduction of new or significantly improved products, services, processes, business models or organizational practices, aimed at simultaneously creating economic, environmental and social value within a long-term perspective . Formula of the slide Sustainable innovation = Innovation + economic value + environmental value + social value , over the long term , for a variety of internal and external stakeholders . 4 essential elements There must be genuine innovation . It is not just about technology . It is collaborative and open innovation. It aims to improve multiple dimensions of the organization’s performance. Context: the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the 2030 Agenda, which balance the economic, social and environmental dimensions (Suchek et al., 2021). 02 Base Innovation: the classic approach Term Course definition Idea – discovery Finding out what was unknown but pre-existing Invention Relies on principles, ideas, theories; often enclosed in R&D labs; can stay disconnected from the market and remain an idea forever Innovation Every phase from prototype development to market launch . Schumpeter: invention = realization of a new resource for the company; innovation = integration of this resource in a product/service offered to the market Main idea: not all ideas lead to innovation (a new product/service delivered to the market). There is no consensus on a single definition. Schumpeter (1912, The Theory of Economic Development ) — 5 sources of innovation Production of a new merchandise A new manufacturing method of an old merchandise Exploitation of a new raw material source Conquest of a new market Reorganization of a production system The entrepreneur’s role = “transforming the production routine, by exploiting an invention or an original technical possibility”. N. Alter (2000): any activity, product or service that questions, more or less deeply, the rules, frameworks and norms (institutional, professional, regulatory…) of a field. Van de Ven (1986): a new idea, possibly a recombination of old ideas, a scheme that challenges the present order, or a formula perceived as new by those involved. Perspective Innovation is… Firm What creates distinctive value to consolidate a competitive position or create a new market User / customer A shift in behaviour and associated values Other stakeholders Only possible if they believe in it and support the firm and the user (suppliers, distribution, financiers, prescribers) Where does innovation lie? Manufacturing methods · development process · cooperation between departments (managerial innovation) · exploitation of new components · new ideas (invention). Innovation is systemic : it requires innovating in several domains. Exemple du cours — Renault 4 electric Dimension Renault 4 e-tech New commodity New electric city car New production method Concurrent engineering, lean management, new design and simulation software Source of components Electric vehicle, material innovations (stronger, lighter) New markets New customer segments, new sales channels Managerial reorganization Project teams, labeling/compliance teams, partnerships Partnerships 4 start-ups: Aura Aero (electric plane), Carapate Aventure (mini-caravan), Ateliers HeritageBike (electric bikes/motorbikes), Searider (electric jet ski) Optional readings: Post-it® history, Swatch Group history. 03 Distinction Incremental vs radical innovation Incremental Radical What Improves performance of an existing product/service Simultaneously and completely alters the technological, societal and market reference points; a break with the existing standard Usage New features do not fundamentally alter purchase/usage patterns Usage conditions change; must be adopted by customers → higher risk Impact Does not disrupt market or organization Result of technological breakthroughs (technical mastery + deep market understanding linked) Origin Continuous improvement process; keeps the firm ahead of imitators Increasingly from new societal and civic expectations (responsible, social, sustainable innovation) Why distinguish them? Strategic: firms build new markets with radical innovation and sustain them against imitators with incremental innovation; radical innovation shows dynamism and opens new growth. Managerial: proves the firm can reinvent itself and integrate new ideas and external skills; motivates teams. Exemple du cours — Kim & Mauborgne (INSEAD), out of 100 innovations Share of innovations Revenues Profits Radical 14% 38% 61% Incremental 86% 62% 39% → Radical innovations have a disproportionate impact on performance. sociology-social-transformations-managem: Idée centrale AI does not make humans obsolete: it raises the price of the skills it cannot perform (judgment, interpretation, meaning, responsibility). To resist cognitive delegation you need a discipline that trains you to question the obvious: sociology . 01 Contexte Course set-up & exam Exam: case studies & group works 40% (continuous collective control: group case study in the last session) · individual exam 60% (multiple-choice questionnaire on Learn). 5 sessions: 1 Introduction & Sociology · 2 Anthropology · 3 Economics · 4 Philosophy · 5 Final session. Aim: form enlightened managers capable of critical distance , not technicians. The humanities are “the discipline of judgment”: the trained capacity to step back, interpret and decide well. Intelligence (slide etymology): inter = between, legere = to choose/pick/gather/read → the ability to “choose between”: sort information, make connections/distinctions, tell true from false and important from unimportant. Questions to keep in mind (slide 11) What intelligence cannot AI replace? Why do democracies need critical thinking? What does sociology let us see that dashboards do not? Opening question (slide 8): “Where else do we already trust systems we don’t understand?” 5 transformations (not one) Technological (AI, data, automation) · Environmental (climate, water, resources) · Geopolitical (fragmentation, tensions) · Economic (inflation, supply chains, volatility) · Societal (meaning, work, identity). 3 pressures of our era Rise of AI: authority shifts from people to systems. Acceleration: speed crowds out reflection and meaning. Fragile debate: shared facts and reasoned argument are under strain. 02 Concepts Episteme, technē, phronēsis, praxis Term Course definition Episteme Universal, theoretical knowledge; science and its laws Technē Craft and know-how, the “how”. AI scales this almost infinitely Phronēsis Practical wisdom: deliberating well and acting rightly in a singular situation. AI cannot supply it Praxis Practical application of a theory, skill or idea, as distinguished from the theory itself Wager of the course: a business school excels at technē; the humanities cultivate the phronēsis AI cannot replace. “Techniques answer how . The humanities answer why .” Exemple du cours — New York, 2023 A lawyer filed a brief written with an AI chatbot citing six prior decisions. None existed (hallucination); no human checked; he was sanctioned. The text was fluent, confident and plausible; what was missing was human judgment: “is this true?” AI is brilliant at… …but this needs a human Automating calculation Judgment Acting at high speed Giving things meaning Processing information Interpreting it Predicting from the past Taking responsibility 03 Auteurs Thinking about intelligence and decision Author Idea Why it matters / hook Turing (1950) By-passed “can machines think?” with the imitation game: if a machine’s text is indistinguishable from a human’s, treat it as intelligent Intelligence defined by performance , not inner understanding; chatbots pass casual versions Simon Bounded rationality: humans satisfice (good-enough under limited time/information). AI optimizes a defined objective The machine optimizes the objective you give; it can’t say if it’s the right one. The hard human part = defining the problem and goal Aristotle Phronēsis: situated, judgment-laden wisdom of acting well in a particular case, distinct from technē and epistēmē; cannot be reduced to a formula Tacit knowledge, expert intuition and phronēsis = human judgment that can’t be reduced to explicit rules. Management = applied phronēsis more than applied technē Gigerenzer Simple heuristics often beat complex models in genuinely uncertain environments. Fast is not always wrong Not “slow good, fast bad”: choosing the right thinking mode is the meta-skill Rosa Social acceleration (technology, pace of life, social change) buys no extra meaning → alienation (“running just to stay in place”). Antidote: resonance , which requires time Meaning needs time; the manager’s edge is slowing down at the right moment Arendt Cognition (problem-solving, which machines do) vs thinking (inner dialogue judging meaning and right/wrong) Delegating thinking is how ordinary competent people enable terrible outcomes. The dashboard can do your cognition, never your thinking Exemple du cours — Zillow Offers (2021) An algorithm priced and bought homes at scale and optimized its target (predicted price) almost perfectly; nobody asked if it was the right target as the market turned. Zillow overpaid for thousands of homes, took a ~$500M write-down and shut the unit. Exemple du cours — Air Canada chatbot (2024) The chatbot invented a bereavement-fare refund. The airline argued the bot was “responsible for its own actions”; a tribunal held the airline liable: a company owns whatever its systems tell customers. Exemple du cours — HFT on Euronext Algorithms trade in microseconds; “flash” events erase value in minutes before a human can grasp what happened. 3 classic managerial mistakes Confusing data with decision-making Optimising the wrong problem Delegating judgement Hook: the real skill is knowing which task is the machine’s and which is yours. Question to bear in mind (slide 25) “In your future role, what will you refuse to delegate?” (no answer given in the course) Cas de classe 1 — The AI CEO (pas de corrigé dans le cours) AI recommends closing a French plant and moving production to Asia (predicts €18m annual savings, +2.5 margin points; flags 420 jobs eliminated, higher transport emissions, geopolitical and supply-chain risks). Questions: what can AI calculate? What can it not decide? What information is missing? Who is responsible? Key line: the numbers are AI’s; the decision and its consequences are yours. Cas de classe 2 — L’Oréal candidate (pas de corrigé) L’Oréal uses AI tools including Seedlink (tested in China): candidates answer open questions, the algorithm assesses fit with desired competencies. AI does not make the final hiring decision; the recruiter does (quoted source: Eva Azouley, 2019, HR VP / Talent Acquisition director, L’Oréal). Questions on bias, override, accountability, and “what does responsible judgment actually mean?”. 04 Sociologie Birth and founders of sociology Why sociology appeared in the 19th century: Industrial Revolution (urbanization, factory labour, new classes) + Democratic Revolution (old order of estates collapses; equality becomes the horizon) → new question: what holds a society together once tradition and hierarchy no longer do? Sociology = “the science that makes the familiar strange and frees us from the obvious” (emancipation from obviousness). Author Core idea Managerial hook Comte Created the word “sociology”; founded positivism (study society with the rigour of natural science). Law of three stages: theological → metaphysical → positive (scientific) Manage society and firms with evidence, not dogma Tocqueville Democracy in America : irreversible rise of equality of conditions; new risk = individualism (retreat into private life) Disengaged individualism is an organizational risk (“quiet quitting”) Marx History driven by class struggle; economic infrastructure (relations of production) shapes the superstructure (law, politics, ideas); alienation; ideology makes an order look natural and eternal. Ancestor of the structural camp Ask whose interests a “neutral” corporate norm serves Durkheim Key concepts of the course: solidarity, the collective consciousness and anomie. Social facts = ways of acting/thinking external to individuals that exert constraint (language, law, morality); method: “treat social facts as things”. Mechanical → organic solidarity (likeness → interdependence/division of labour). Anomie ( a nomos ) and Suicide (1897) Anomie explains crises in firms after brutal change Weber Understand the meaning actors give their conduct; ideal types; four types of social action. sustainable-innovation/01-eco-design-des: Message clé de la séance An innovation is not sustainable simply because the product is better designed. It becomes sustainable when the value proposition , the value chain and the business model are consistent with the sustainability objective. Key question: how can we move from a commitment to sustainability to a concrete, viable innovation that is consistent with the entire value chain? 01 Définition Eco-design Eco-design (sustainable design) — course definition An approach that aims, right from the initial phases of the innovation process (imagination, creativity, problem framing), to satisfy a need or function while reducing environmental impacts, creating social value, and ensuring economic viability across the entire life cycle of the new product or service and for all its stakeholders . It leads us to rethink not only the product or service, but also its usage, associated services, value chain and business model . Inspired by: Steux & Aggeri (2021) ; Prendeville et al. (2017) ; Spangenberg et al. (2010). 4 key points Consider the entire life cycle . Move from a purely environmental focus to sustainability . Move from the product to a product-service offering . Move from the product (or service) to a systemic approach that includes internal and external factors. Ecodesign — definition in Prendeville et al. (2017) A collaborative, proactive and systematic design and management process that considers the full life-cycle environmental impacts of packaging, products, processes, services, organisations and systems. It is a life-cycle management approach that avoids uncoordinated product planning: e.g. eliminating a toxic substance should not lead to higher energy consumption. 02 Modèle Design thinking — standard approach Design Thinking (course definition) A discipline that uses the sensitivity, tools and methods of designers to enable interdisciplinary teams to innovate by matching desirability (user expectations), technological feasibility and economic viability . Principles: Structured method in 5 key steps . Based on understanding the customer experience and its uses to imagine an innovative solution. Combines desirability, feasibility and viability. Continuous experiential approach: develop hypotheses → prototype and experiment (real object, real or virtual model, diagram, drawing…). Uses personas . Used by a team as open and diversified as possible (internal services, customers, partners…). Step What you do Guiding question (slide) 1. Empathize Learn about the audience by observation and interview Who is my user? What matters to this person? 2. Define Create a point of view based on user needs and insights What are their needs? 3. Ideate Brainstorm, as many creative solutions as possible (wild ideas encouraged) — 4. Prototype Build a representation of one or more ideas to show others How can I show my idea? A prototype is just a rough draft! 5. Test Share the prototype with the original user for feedback What worked? What didn’t? The 3 pillars Ideas, hypotheses, prototypes and experiments are evaluated and retained at all times against three pillars : Desirability (consumer expectations) · Feasibility (functional and achievable in the foreseeable future) · Viability / Sustainability (fits into a sustainable business model). Incohérence dans le cours The slide lists the third pillar as “ Sustainability ” but the Venn diagram and the definition say “ Viability (business / economic)”. Both are shown in the slides; the definition and Brown/Baldassarre use viability . Check with the professor which word is expected. Tools: persona and prototypes Persona : an imaginary character representing a target group or segment. Usually has a first name and social and psychological characteristics. Several personas can be used in one project; it can be shown as a storyboard of use. Prototypes , models, objects in progress: visualize and make uses concrete · experiment, test, evaluate · tell “a story” (shared vocabulary) · foster participation of all. Exemple du cours — Persona Mrs Isabelle, 78, lives alone, enjoys reading and the theatre, degrading health. Expectation: to have friends. Constraint: lives in an isolated village. Exemple du cours — Accor DT approaches are based on trust between participants. They require recognising the competence of teams . They are not compatible with the top-down managerial culture that often prevails. They are not solely focused on the end user, and not solely inspired by the engineers’ culture of finding a solution to the question posed. AccorHotels set up Labs in certain hotels to devise solutions with DT. + Contexte History (slide dates) 1950s — Alex Osborn, brainstorming. 1960s — Stanford, first interdepartmental, human-centred Product Design programme. 1987 — Peter Rowe, book “Design Thinking” (MIT Press). 1991 — IDEO founded in Palo Alto (David Kelley): decompartmentalization, dynamism, questioning. 1999 — IDEO creates a new supermarket shopping cart in 5 days (ABC News challenge), with designers, doctors, logisticians… 2000 — more publications, symposia, courses · 2001 — IDEO from 20 to 500 employees · 2012 — 3 Design Thinking schools (Ponts et Chaussées Paris, Beijing, Tokyo). 03 Critique Design thinking: interests and limits for eco-design The slide poses the question (“Interests? Limits / key considerations?”) without giving an answer . The answers below come from the mandatory articles , not from the slide. Limit of standard DT (Baldassarre et al., 2024) Consequence Core assumption (from Brown 2008 and Martin 2009): DT supports organisations in gaining competitive advantage by balancing desirability, feasibility, viability Focus on economic impact: of 115 articles reviewed, 90% economic (104), 40% social (46), only 7% environmental (8) Feasibility and viability = technical and financial; desirability = what individuals want Social and environmental impacts are not part of the “equation”; individual wants can conflict with collective interest (e.g. new smartphone each year) Environmental and social effects treated as acceptable externalities Negative impacts in practice 04 Article Responsible design thinking (Baldassarre et al., 2024) New assumption proposed Design thinking is an approach that supports organisations in collaboratively addressing the challenges of sustainable development , by considering desirability, feasibility and viability within responsible innovation processes and outcomes that are ethically acceptable for society and the environment . Responsibility becomes the overarching criterion: what is ethically acceptable for society and the environment. Phase (Double Diamond) DT practice Responsible innovation dimension Outcome Discovery Framing → reflective framing Reflexivity Responsible policies Definition Envisioning → anticipatory envisioning Anticipation Responsible project ideas Development Co-creating → inclusive co-creating Inclusion Responsible coalitions of organisations Delivery Prototyping → responsive prototyping Responsiveness Responsible products and services Responsible innovation = experimental and collaborative approach of adaptive learning to solve wicked problems, with an ethical focus on economic, social and environmental impacts. Reflexivity : dialogue to go beyond individual perspectives. Anticipation : think systemically, foresee plausible and desirable outcomes. Inclusion : involve a broader range of stakeholders. Responsiveness : adjust shape and direction as knowledge emerges. Responsible prototyping is “a long marathon”, not a short sprint. Exemple de l’article — Fairphone vs. orthodox DT Apple and Samsung are used as cases of balancing desirability, feasibility, viability while ignoring environmental and social impacts. Fairphone treats human rights and resource depletion as cornerstones: fair value chain, upgradable and durable design, brand that nudges consumers to reconsider what they need. consumer-behavior-customer-experience-ma: Idée centrale The course follows one logic, session after session: understand the consumer first, then see how brands turn that understanding into a unique, memorable experience (CB focus → CEM focus). 01 Organisation Course set-up, evaluation & rules Objectives: understand consumer behaviour (internal psychological dynamics: decision-making, motivation, perception, learning and memory, identity; external social and cultural influences: family, communities, tribes) · connect theory and customer experience management · develop a critical perspective on how companies design and stage experiences, including the ethical boundaries of experience engineering (e.g. sensory manipulation) · apply through case studies and a group research project (Poster Fair). Session Topic CB focus CEM focus Case / project 1 From understanding consumers to designing experiences Decision-making, motivation, involvement & attitude Intro to CX & the Experience Economy Group project intro, brand/store choice 2 Perception, learning & memory Affective and cognitive dimensions of experience Sensory marketing; products as memory makers Case study — Aesop (skincare) 3 The self, personality & identity How consumption shapes who we are (symbolic consumption) Extended self & self-empowerment through brands Case study — On (running) 4 Social & cultural influences Family, communities, tribes, subcultures & countercultures Brand communities & tribal marketing Case study — A24 5 Poster Fair & individual exam — — 1h30 + 1h30 Evaluation Content 60% individual “Written” exam 50% : short case study, same format as in-class group case studies, 1h30 · Participation 10% : attendance 4 points per session + oral participation up to 4 bonus points 40% group Group project: poster & videography, presented at the Poster Fair (1h30). +2 bonus points for groups who performed well on the in-class case studies Rules KEDGE rule: more than 2 unexcused absences → no admission to the final exam. AI policy: generative AI is permitted for the group project only , if used responsibly and transparently (acknowledge any AI content, keep a log of prompts/sources/decisions; the fieldwork must be your own). Not permitted for in-class case studies or the final exam. Reference books (only “for those who want to dig deeper”): Solomon & Russell (2024), Schmitt (2003), Pine & Gilmore (2019), Carù & Cova (2007). 02 Définition What is consumer behaviour? Consumer Behaviour (CB) The study of the processes involved when individuals or groups select, purchase, use or dispose of products, services, ideas or experiences to satisfy needs and desires and to define and express their identities . An inherently interdisciplinary field: it explains not just what consumers buy but why . Discipline Contribution Limit (slide) Economics Utility & rationality Ignores social/qualitative factors Anthropology Rituals, myths & symbols Overlooks ethics Psychology (most influential in CB) Decision-making, motivation, perception, learning, the self and personality: the individual mind Leaves the social context out Sociology (growing influence, notably Consumer Culture Theory) Social forces: family, communities, tribes, sub/countercultures Captures the collective dynamics psychology cannot Unpacking the definition The process What we study Who we study Need recognition → search for information → pre-purchase evaluation of alternatives → product choice, purchase & consumption → post-consumption evaluation Selecting · purchasing/obtaining (buying, receiving, inheriting) · using (consuming, wearing, storing) · disposing (giving, recycling, reselling) · expressing identity Individuals (sensibility, self-concept, personality, identity; different individuals can play different roles) and groups (families, communities, tribes; one or several people may shape a decision many will use) 03 Pourquoi Why study CB & link with marketing Key message If you don’t understand your audience, you can market what you perceive as the best product ever — and still not sell it. Exemple du cours — The New Coke story 1975: the Pepsi Challenge. 1985: New Coke (“Change for the best!”) → back to Coca-Cola Classic just 79 days later . 2019: Stranger Things (season 3): Coca-Cola turns its worst year into a pop-culture moment. Marketing (American Marketing Association) An organizational function and a set of processes for creating, communicating and delivering value to customers and for managing customer relationships in ways that benefit the organization and its stakeholders. The study of consumers is at the core. Marketing step Tools Where the consumer is Strategic planning (environment, industry & internal analyses) Porter’s 5 Forces, PESTEL → SWOT The ‘S’ in PESTEL = socio-cultural trends → emerging consumer behaviours. Porter’s Buyer Power = consumers’ influence over pricing, quality, market conditions Strategic process & branding Market (consumer) studies, segmenting, targeting & positioning Positioning : how a product/brand is perceived in the minds of consumers, relative to competitors Marketing mix 4 P’s (product, price, place, promotion) 4 Cs (consumer’s view): consumer solution, consumer cost, convenience, communication — think through the 4 Cs, then build the 4 P’s on that platform Control Measuring, evaluating, corrective actions — How do we study consumers? Not a methodology course, but useful to know where concepts come from: Approach Methods Observation Natural/artificial settings · in-home observation · shadowing · physiological methods (eye-tracking) Interviews & surveys Individual interviews (small sample, exploratory, or large sample for surveys) · focus groups · longitudinal studies (panels, scanner data) Experimentation Cause-and-effect: manipulate independent variables (e.g. number of ads, package design) to measure dependent variables (purchase intent or behaviour) · lab vs field experiments 04 Tendances Trends that shape consumer behaviour today Trend Key ideas Symbolic consumption People often buy brands not for what they do but for what they mean . Brands build entire symbolic universes (“branded world”: story, aesthetics, ritual). McCracken’s Meaning Transfer Model (1986): meaning moves from culture → to the brand (advertising, design) → to the consumer (how they use, wear, talk about it). Consumers choose brands consistent with their needs, personality and sense of self Pop culture Music, movies, sports, books, celebrities consumed by the mass market. Meets brands at different depths: celebrity endorsement · product placement → branded entertainment · merchandise from strong creative/cultural brands. Marketing doesn’t just borrow from pop culture — it should learn FROM it Social media Shift from one-way messaging to a “horizontal revolution”. Redistributes trust (user-generated content shapes perceptions as much as advertising) and compresses the decision process (discovery, evaluation, purchase in one flow) Data analytics Massive consumer data (transactions, GPS, clicks, social activity) analysed by algorithms → turns behaviour into a resource ; marketing moves from reactive to anticipatory Artificial intelligence Machine-learning systems inside everyday interactions. Personalizes the choice environment at scale : many small choices are pre-filtered by algorithms → how much of what we “choose” is still our own? Idée centrale Money received at different dates cannot be compared directly. To compare “apples with apples”, we bring every amount to the same point in time : forward (future value) or backward (present value). 01 Notion Why money has a time value Inflation : in 5 years, the same €100 may buy fewer goods. Investment : €100 today invested 1 year at 10% becomes €110. The extra €10 is the return (here, the interest). Exemple du cours A generous uncle offers €100: today or in 5 years. Most people choose today. Definitions Future value (FV) : the value that a current amount of money will have at a future date after earning interest. Present value (PV) : the value today of an amount of money to be received or paid in the future. With 10%: €100 today → €110 in one year (FV). €100 received in one year is worth \(100/1.10 \approx 90.90\) today (PV). 02 Notion Why interest rates exist Impatience (“myopia”): people prefer to use money today; the future is valued less than the present. Opportunity cost of waiting : a lender who lends €100 cannot use it. The interest compensates this wait (lend €100, get €110 → €10 of interest). Inflation : higher inflation → the lender requires a higher rate. Fisher effect Nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation. Exemple du cours Real return wanted 4%, expected inflation 6% → nominal rate of about 10%. 03 Notion Simple vs compound interest Simple interest Compound interest Interest is… not reinvested (spent) reinvested: interest earns interest €100 at 10%, 3 years €10 per year → €30 of interest in total €110 → €121 → €133.10 Where used specific contexts: trust funds, charitable organizations, university endowments (principal untouched, only the income is spent) the usual way financial markets work Future value (compound) \[ FV = PV \times (1+i)^n \] Example du cours : \( 100 \times 1.10^3 = 133.10 \). The exponent is the number of periods. Present value \[ PV = \dfrac{FV}{(1+i)^n} \] Example du cours : \( 121 / 1.10^2 = 100 \). Banks use present value calculations to set loans: the payments happen in the future, but they must be related to the amount lent today. 04 Méthode Timelines & multiple cash flows Method Draw a timeline (year 0, 1, 2, 3…). Move each cash flow separately to the chosen date (compound it forward or discount it back). Add the results. Exemple du cours — future value €100 today and €100 in year 1, rate 10%, value in year 2: \(100\times1.10^2 = 121\) and \(100\times1.10 = 110\) → €231 . The interest earned on the first €100 is reinvested (compound interest). The second €100 earns interest for one year only. Exemple du cours — present value €100 in year 1 and €100 in year 2, rate 10%: \(100/1.10 = 90.90\) and \(100/1.10^2 = 82.64\) → €173.54 . With €173.54 invested at 10% today, you can pay €100 in year 1 and €100 in year 2. The amounts don’t have to be equal (€60, €42, €100…). Each has a different value depending on when it is received: this is the common reference point for CFOs and finance teams evaluating projects. 05 Notion Annuities Annuity Equal (constant) cash flows at regular intervals. Most loans are annuities: mortgage loans, business loans, many standard bank loans. Notation in the course: A (or a ) = regular payment, i = interest rate, n = number of periods. Spreadsheet names: PVA (present value of an annuity), FVA (future value of an annuity), PMT (payment). The logic is: PVA = sum of the present values of each payment. The spreadsheet exercises use the Excel functions above. Computation check below uses that logic. Understanding rule (professor): understand how it works and what each element represents ; experiment in Excel by changing payment, rate or periods. 06 Distinction APR vs EAR APR (annual percentage rate) EAR (effective annual rate) What it is Annual rate used to derive the periodic rate . Information in the loan contract, not the rate you really pay. The rate you actually pay per year , once compounding is taken into account. Link Periodic rate = APR / number of periods (monthly: APR/12 ; daily: APR/365) Compound the periodic rate over the periods of one year, then subtract the €1 borrowed Size Smaller Bigger (the gap can be significant) In France Taux débiteur annuel — both must be declared, but the APR is the one most cited because it is smaller TAEG (taux annuel effectif global) — lets you compare offers Conversions (course method) \[ APR = \text{periodic rate} \times \text{number of periods per year} \] \[ EAR = (1+\text{periodic rate})^{m} - 1 \quad (m = \text{periods per year}) \] EAR method of the professor: borrow €1 for the 12 months (or 365 days) at the periodic rate, compute the future value (compounding), subtract the €1 borrowed. sociology-social-transformations-managem: Idée centrale Session 1 ended on: society is constructed, the social order could be otherwise. How is it held together? Through shared meaning: myths, rites and doctrines — and so do companies. “Myth founds. Rites enact. Doctrine fixes. Remove any one and meaning destabilizes.” 01 Introduction Why anthropology for managers Object of anthropology The surplus over the useful : graduations, weddings, integration weekends or conventions (costumes, repeated words, precise order, photographs) are not “useful” in a technical sense, yet the group feels something essential is missing without them. Humans don’t merely act: they give their actions meaning . Anthropology = “the science of human meaning”; beneath every “obvious” practice lies a symbolic system. 3 reasons it matters A firm is not only a value machine: it is a community of meaning ; people commit or quit largely for symbolic reasons. Strategy and change fail more often on culture (meaning) than on spreadsheets (technique). Anthropology gives the rarest skill: reading and shaping your organization’s symbolic order deliberately. Key questions: Why do humans need myths? How do rites structure collective life? What role does doctrine play in stabilizing meaning? The core (master these) The gallery (context only) Lévi-Strauss (culture/nature) · Geertz (webs of meaning) · Durkheim (belonging & rites) · van Gennep (passage) · Schein (the iceberg) Anthropology: Tylor, Cassirer, Durand, Mauss, Étienne · Myth: Eliade, Barthes, Girard · Rites & doctrine: van Gennep, Goffman, Douglas, Bourdieu Reading tip: follow the triptych “Myth · Rites · Doctrine”, not the roll-call of names. 02 Partie 1 Humans: meaning-seeking, belonging-seeking, symbol-making Author Idea Why it matters / managerial hook Tylor (1871) First definition of culture: the whole of knowledge, belief, art, morals, law and custom acquired as a member of society. Culture is learned and shared, not biological. (Frazer’s Golden Bough launched the comparative study of myth and ritual — magic → religion → science; later criticized as ethnocentric) “Talent” is often culture (learned codes) mistaken for nature (innate gift) Lévi-Strauss Nature = the given and universal; culture = the constructed and variable. Under diversity the mind structures the world through binary oppositions (raw/cooked, sacred/profane). Culture is order imposed on the world “That’s just how our industry works” is a cultural claim disguised as natural law Cassirer Humans are less rational than animal symbolicum (symbol-making animal); we live through symbolic forms: language, myth, art, religion, science We live in a universe of meaning, not just facts. To manage humans is to manage symbols (a logo, a title, a corner office) Geertz Culture = the web of meanings humans themselves have spun; the analyst’s task is interpretation of what it means to people, not only what they do A symbolic system is a shared code turning basic behaviour into meaning. “A promotion is 5% salary and 95% symbol” Durand The imaginary is not idle fantasy opposed to reason: it is the deep structuring activity of the mind, the reservoir of images, symbols and myths through which we make the world meaningful and confront our oldest fear, time and death It is the engine of myth; its “regimes” explain why a culture/company is fascinated by heroic conquest or by solidarity. Is your brand story diurnal (disruption, the hero) or nocturnal (care, community)? Durkheim Humans need to belong to something larger; when bonds and shared norms dissolve → anomie , disorientation, distress Meaning and belonging are conditions of psychic survival. Disengagement is often anomie — a broken bond, not a lazy individual Mauss ( The Gift , 1925) Archaic exchange runs not on price but on a triple obligation: give · receive · reciprocate . The gift is a total social fact (economic, moral, religious at once) that weaves the social bond Reciprocity, not just contracts, holds groups together (gift economy vs market). Recognition is a gift; un-reciprocated effort breaks the bond Étienne (anthropologist of religion, Sciences Po Aix) Secularization does not erase the sacred, it displaces it. Disenchanted societies (Weber) reinvest the sacred in politics, sport, consumption, ecology… and organizations The need for the sacred/symbolic is structural; it “seeks new altars” — the key to “corporate religion”. A strong culture can build devotion or tip into a cult Part 1 takeaway Humans are meaning-seeking, belonging-seeking, symbol-making animals. Societies cohere not by force or interest alone but by shared meaning. Question de classe (pas de corrigé) “In your opinion, what kind of imaginary does the word ‘KEDGE’ conjure up?” 03 Partie 2 The triptych: myth · rites · doctrine MYTH RITES DOCTRINE Question What story are we part of? How do we enact & renew it? What must we believe & obey? Content Founding narratives, origins, heroes, missions Repeated symbolic actions: integration, cohesion, legitimacy Explicit rules & beliefs: the allowed, forbidden, valued Verb founds enact fixes Myth A myth is not a “false story” A foundational narrative that gives a group its origin, identity and direction . Its truth is not factual but meaning-bearing. Myths answer what data never can: where do we come from, who are we, where are we going? They are the deep code of identity . Hook: strip a company of its founding story and its “values” become empty slogans. Eliade: myths tell of the origin (“in the beginning”), anchoring the present in a sacred founding moment that rituals periodically re-actualize; to found is to give a cosmogony. Hook: anniversaries and “founding day” rituals. Lévi-Strauss: myth is a machine for resolving contradictions a society cannot otherwise resolve (life/death, nature/culture); meaning lies in the structure of relations, not the surface plot (“myths think themselves in men”). Hook: a corporate saga often reconciles profit vs purpose. Barthes ( Mythologies , 1957): myth moved into advertising, brands and mass culture; its trick is turning the cultural/historical into the “natural” and self-evident (the new Citroën as a modern goddess). Myth is a type of speech that hides its own construction — exactly what a critical manager must learn to see through. Hook: a brand myth makes a commercial promise feel like a natural truth. Girard: groups are bound by mimetic desire (we want what others want) ⇒ rivalry ⇒ crisis resolved by designating a scapegoat whose expulsion restores unity; founding myths often conceal this founding violence. Beneath unity there is sometimes an expelled victim; recognizing the pattern is “moral lucidity”. Hook: after a crisis, watch for the “scapegoat executive” sacrificed to restore calm. Rites Rite A codified, repeated symbolic action that enacts shared meaning. If myth is the story, the rite is the performance that makes it real and renews it. Four functions: 1. integration (we belong) · 2. cohesion (we are one) · 3. legitimacy (this is official) · 4. safe transition (change without chaos). Hook: you cannot transmit culture by memo, only by repeated, embodied rites. van Gennep (1909): every change of status follows 3 phases — separation (you leave the old status) · liminality (the in-between threshold) · reincorporation (you enter the new status). Birth, initiation, marriage, retirement. Transitions are dangerous; rites carry people across safely and visibly. Hook: onboarding and promotions — design the three phases. Durkheim: gathered in ritual, individuals feel a shared energy, collective effervescence , fusing them into a moral community. Religion = society worshipping itself; rites renew the bond and recharge the sacred (set apart from the profane). Hook: the annual convention is engineered effervescence. Goffman: daily life is full of micro-rites (greetings, “face-work”, deference, demeanor) protecting each person’s dignity and keeping the interaction order running. Hook: the standup, Monday meeting, after-

Idée centrale Capital budgeting = decision process corporations use when they invest capital in new ventures: the comparison of costs versus future profits (advertising campaign, R&D, acquiring a competitor…). 01 Méthode Criteria & standard steps Criteria most often used: NPV , IRR , Profitability Index (PI) , Payback Period (“not so good”), Discounted Payback Period . Standard steps Estimate CFs (inflows & outflows). Assess riskiness of CFs. Determine the cost of capital i for the project. Find NPV and/or IRR and/or PI. Accept if NPV > 0 and/or IRR > WACC and/or PI > 1 . 02 Critère Net Present Value (NPV) Definition NPV = Present Value minus the monetary value of the initial investment (“Net” because the initial investment is taken into account). For a project: the value of the income generated in excess of the initial investment (cost of the project). The discount rate i is generally the cost of capital appropriate for the company and its project. Formula \[ NPV = \sum_{t=0}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t} = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{CF_t}{(1+i)^t} + CF_0 \] \(i\) = discount rate · \(CF_t\) = cash flow at time t · \(CF_0\) = initial investment (usually a negative number) NPV = PV inflows − PV of cost = net gain in wealth. Decision rule NPV > 0 : PV of the income stream is greater than the cost → accept (above-normal profits). NPV < 0 : cost is greater than the income stream → reject . Properties: the most used criterion · considers the time value of money · absolute measure of wealth (positive NPVs increase the owner’s wealth, negative ones decrease it) · discount rate = cost of capital · project CFs are assumed reinvested at the cost of capital. How a firm can generate above-normal profits: buyers’ preference for established brand names · control of distribution systems · patent control · exclusive ownership of superior natural resources · access to lower-cost financial resources · economies of scale · access to superior labor or management talents. Exemple du cours — Project A, WACC = 10% CFs: −100 (t=0), 10, 60, 80. PVs: 9.09 + 49.59 + 60.11 = 118.79 (rounded), so NPV A ≈ 18.79 → positive → accept. (Unrounded: 18.78.) Excel trap (from the exercises’ tip) NPV(rate, range) discounts the first value by one period. So write =NPV(rate, CF1:CFn)+CF0 . IRR needs the full range including time 0 . 03 Notion NPV and the discount rate The higher the discount rate, the smaller the NPV (everything else equal); the smaller the rate, the larger the NPV. consumer-behavior-customer-experience-ma: Idée centrale The brain processes sensory stimuli along two dimensions — cognitive (mental processing) and affective (emotional response) — before any meaning is assigned . Consumers want more than function: they want an experience , which puts product design, packaging and store atmospherics at the centre of strategy. Memorable experiences are those that are sensory-rich, emotionally charged and personally relevant . 01 Processus Perception: from sensation to interpretation Term Course definition Sensation The biochemical signals our senses send to the brain. Sensory receptors (eyes, ears, nose, mouth, fingers, skin) capture basic stimuli (light, colour, sound, odour, texture) Perception The process by which people select, organize and interpret sensations. It studies what we add to the raw sensations to give them meaning The three stages Exposure → Attention → Interpretation (stimuli: sights, sounds, smells, tastes, textures → receptors: eyes, ears, nose, mouth, skin). Exemples du cours (slide 5) The iconic Orangina bottle (designed by Jean-Claude Beton, 1936) · Jo Malone’s flagship scent bar in London (designed for hands-on fragrance discovery) · the Kit Kat street campaign (2016): a bench designed to look and feel like the chocolate bar. 02 Étape 1 Exposure & sensory thresholds Exposure Occurs when a stimulus comes within range of the sensory receptors . We can concentrate, ignore, or completely miss stimuli. Threshold Definition Absolute threshold (seuil) The minimum amount of stimulation a person can detect on a given sensory channel Differential threshold The ability of a sensory system to detect changes or differences between two stimuli . The minimum detectable difference = the j.n.d. (just noticeable difference) Exemple du cours — absolute thresholds Sense Threshold Vision A candle flame 30 miles away Hearing A watch ticking 20 feet away Smell A drop of perfume in a six-room house Taste A teaspoon of sugar in a gallon of water Touch A fly’s wing on your cheek, dropped from 1 cm Slide image next to the differential threshold: the Pepsi logos from 1898 to 2005 (no commentary given). Thresholds are not fixed They vary from person to person (biological differences: age, genetics, sensory acuity) and with context and attention. Use: design logos, packaging, scents and sounds that are perceptible without being overwhelming . The myth of subliminal perception A stimulus below the absolute threshold is called subliminal (Vicary, 1957: “Hungry? Eat popcorn”). The idea has fascinated the public for 50+ years. No evidence that subliminal perception has any effect on consumer behaviour : a stimulus below the absolute threshold never even reaches the sensory receptors, so it cannot be processed, let alone influence behaviour. 03 Étape 2 Attention & perceptual selection In a cluttered media environment we suffer sensory overload : far more information than we can process. Marketers must break through the noise (original content, teaser campaigns, unexpected formats). Slide examples: Michel & Augustin packaging, a Netflix street campaign near the Arc de Triomphe, an Adidas Originals shoebox pavilion. Attention & perceptual selection Attention = the extent to which processing activity is focused on a particular stimulus . It is selective : consumers process only a small fraction of the stimuli they are exposed to = perceptual selection . Mechanism Definition Example (slide) Perceptual vigilance More likely to notice stimuli related to current needs Shopping for a car → suddenly you notice car ads everywhere Perceptual defense People see what they want to see and screen out what they don’t A heavy smoker mentally blocks images of cancer-scarred lungs Adaptation How long consumers keep noticing a stimulus; once too familiar, they stop paying attention Slide image: roadside billboards 04 Étape 3 Interpretation & semiotics Interpretation The meaning we assign to sensory stimuli: the cognitive process by which we organize and make sense of what our senses capture. We do not interpret in a vacuum: we relate stimuli to prior knowledge stored in memory (past experiences, expectations, personality, cultural background). Primarily cognitive, but often triggers affective/emotional responses. Semiotics Every marketing message has an object (the product), a sign (what represents it) and an interpretant (the meaning we derive). Exemple du cours: object = Nike shoe (brand) · sign = the Swoosh · interpretant = hip-hop culture, urban status symbol. Signs relate to the object in three ways: icon, index, symbol (slide examples: Michelin’s Bibendum = icon · Mr Clean = index · Apple’s apple = symbol). Information absente The slide does not define icon, index and symbol; it only shows one example each. No definition is invented here. 05 CEM Sensory marketing Sensory marketing A strategic approach that targets consumers’ five senses (sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell) to create an emotional connection with a brand or product; sensory stimuli guide perceptions and behaviours. Aim: offer not only a product but a memorable experience (pleasant store smell, relaxing music, tactile quality → more positive feelings and loyalty). Slide examples: Perrier × Philippe Starck bottle; Perrier “Melt, Tennis” campaign (Ogilvy Paris). Experiential marketing Sensory marketing The broader paradigm. Purchasing vs consuming: the transaction is not the experience . Holbrook & Hirschman (1982): fantasies, feelings and fun. Cognitive, behavioural and relational dimensions alongside sensory and emotional aspects Operational: the practical, applied side of the experiential paradigm. Focuses on the five senses: perceptions, sensations and the emotions they trigger → affective, cognitive and behavioural reactions Krishna’s model (2012) Sensation (haptics, olfaction, audition, taste, vision) → perception → emotion and cognition ↔ attitude, learning/memory, behaviour . Sensory stimuli in marketing Sense Marketing stimuli Influence on CB Sights Advertising, store design (colours, lights), packaging (colours, size, styling), logo, “trade dress” Colours carry meanings and elicit strong emotional reactions (biological and cultural); lighting impacts purchasing Smells Ambient scent (store atmospherics) and product scent (“inside” products) Stir emotions, calm, relieve stress or invoke memories ( Proust’s syndrome ), but can also make you feel sick Sounds Jingles, songs, in-store music, slogans — and products Affect feelings, behaviour, and the time and money spent in a store Textures Product or packaging (clothes, furniture, car makers) Haptic senses (→ endowment effect ) affect product experience and judgment Taste Food industry Tastes stir emotions (biological and cultural) 06 Sens 1 Sights: colour, packaging, lighting Colour Meanings (slide) Red prompts action, passion, excitement, strength, love, energy Orange warmth, energy, youthful, confidence, success, bravery, sociability Yellow caution, youthful, creativity, happiness, warmth, cheer Green natural, health, wellbeing, innovative, newness, freshness, quality Blue intelligence, refreshing, luxury, classic, trust, peace, loyalty Pink feminine, youthful, compassion, sincerity, sophistication, sweet Purple elegant, royalty, luxury, spirituality, ambition Brown dependable, rugged, trustworthy, simple Black classic, conventional, formal, dramatic, sophistication, security White pure, calm, clean, simplicity, innocence, honest Slide logos: Carte Bleue/Visa, Starbucks, Barbie. Campbell’s Tomato Soup: made famous by Andy Warhol, whose pop art turned an everyday product into a cultural symbol. sustainable-innovation/02-value-chain-bu: Idée centrale Sustainability must be aligned with positioning, value proposition, resources and every activity of the value chain. A “sustainable” product often fails because the management system (evaluation, bonuses, spare parts) pushes the opposite way. 01 Définition Strategic alignment and sustainability Strategic alignment (sustainable innovation) Ensuring that an organisation’s environmental and social objectives are consistent with its competitive positioning , its value proposition , its resources and capabilities , and all activities across its value chain . This alignment helps create a sustainable competitive advantage . Situation typique (slide 22) “We want to develop sustainable and repairable products.” But: Purchasing staff are assessed solely on price . Engineers are assessed on time-to-market . Sales staff get bonuses on the number of new products sold . Spare parts are not available. → The “sustainable” product conflicts with the company’s management system . 02 Outil Porter’s value chain Value chain The various stages through which an organisation creates value for its customers (Johnson et al., 2011). Core (primary) functions — directly linked to value creation Support functions — improve effectiveness and efficiency of core functions Procurement · Production · Logistics · Marketing · Services (Porter diagram: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service) Technological development · Human resources management · Infrastructure (Porter diagram also shows Procurement among support activities) Écart de classification The text slide lists Procurement as a core function, but the Porter diagram (and the Apple example, “Buying Department” under Support Activities ) puts it in the support activities. Both appear in the slides. What value-chain analysis is used for Describe the company’s operations and activities. Understand the functions through which the company creates value for customers/stakeholders. Does it have a firm grasp of the areas where it creates value? Understand which functions create little value but cost money . Can it reduce costs/margins without risk? Can it externalize the function without risk? Exemple du cours — Apple’s value chain Function Facts in the slides Supply & production Sourcing from several countries/continents; pressure to manufacture fast (risk of obsolescence); seeks new subcontractors for its CSR policy (more recycled materials); production line in China to minimise costs, then shipped to the Californian warehouse Marketing & commercialisation Average product lifespan: 1 year → high storage costs (fast delivery, stock rotation); reduced delivery costs due to high volumes; very high and rising marketing costs: presence on all channels (Apple retail and online stores, mobile network operators, wholesalers, retailers) Service Returns within 14 days if bought from an Apple store (physical or online): very high cost but supports the strategic decision to keep close ties with customers R&D (support) Innovation policy is a key factor of performance; over 26 billion dollars spent on R&D in 2022; major partnerships essential and costly Buying (support) 200 suppliers in 2021; win-win relationship; a supplier not meeting specifications is immediately replaced by a competitor; long-term partnership that contributes directly to R&D and marketing (at a cost) Exemple du cours — IKEA (session 3 link) Moving from a value chain organised around selling new furniture to one that emphasises product lifespan, repair, reuse and material recovery requires transforming the whole value creation system, not just designing greener furniture (see chapter 3). 03 Cas Frugal innovation: CLEAN Home washing machine Case data (class work): manufacturer of “traditional” household appliances, mid-to-high-end. Tech-Cleaning : colour touchscreen; Wi-Fi + mobile app; 18 programmes; automatic detergent dispensing; load sensors; steam programme; variable-speed motor; proprietary electronic components; sophisticated design; 2-year warranty; €849 . Information absente The slides ask to (1) outline the value chain, (2) propose a more frugal solution, (3) list the questions to transform the value chain, but give no definition of “frugal innovation” and no model answer . Nothing is invented here. A practice way to approach it is to apply the value-chain questions above (which activities create little value but cost money? where does the management system conflict with repairability/durability?). 04 Outil Business Model Canvas (BMC) BMC A visual tool used in management and entrepreneurship to describe, design, analyse and concisely represent a company’s business model. Developed by Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur (“Business Model Generation”). A sheet/table divided into nine blocks , best examined in order . The creative process is value-driven : how does value benefit customers (and other stakeholders)? # Block Slide definition 1 Customer segments target users/buyers of your product/service 2 Value proposition the practical relevance for customers 3 Channels communication channels with clients 4 Customer relationships type of interrelation maintained with target customers 5 Revenue streams income-generating model (subscription plans, direct sales…) 6 Key resources assets in demand to keep the business running 7 Key activities actions required for being profitable 8 Key partners entities/individuals involved in activities 9 Cost structure all expenses incl. payroll, rent, etc. Numbering follows the numbers printed on the slide 24 canvas. Exemple du cours — IKEA canvas (slide 26) Includes, e.g., value propositions: sturdy furniture, functional, aesthetics, affordable pricing, food & beverage; customer relationships incl. “sustainable, eco-friendly community”; channels: retail stores, website, app, F&B restaurant; revenue: furniture, F&B, franchise fee. Reminder note on the slide: design is considered “a new way of thinking” combining engineering and creativity, according to Herbert A. Simon, 1969. 05 Article obligatoire Acosta et al. (2014): sustainable business models Article: Acosta, Acquier, Carbone et al. (2014), Les business models du développement durable , L’Expansion Management Review 152(1), 20-29. Objective: how businesses reconcile environmental and social challenges with economic activity. Data: 2013 study (ESCP Europe i7 with weave AIR): interviews with 34 European executives (multinationals to start-ups). Main results Sustainable innovation is not a compromise but an opportunity to optimise economic, social and environmental aspects simultaneously . It must go beyond continuous improvement or sector conventions: a forward-looking strategic vision . Main condition: a fundamental overhaul of the way we innovate and manage innovation to build a sustainable and viable business model. sociology-social-transformations-managem: Idée centrale Economics is not one truth : it is a field of rival theories with political consequences . Each school is a different bet on human nature, markets and the state. Management is applied economics : your (often unspoken) school decides how you lead. 01 Introduction Why economics for managers Where we left off: Session 2 ended on Mauss: exchange began with the gift, not price; the market is one historical form of exchange, not a law of nature. Today’s question: what is “the economy”, and why can brilliant economists read the same facts and reach opposite conclusions? 3 reasons it matters Every tool you’ll use (KPIs, bonuses, transfer prices, “shareholder value”, outsourcing…) is applied economic theory . “Use it blind, and the theory uses you.” Models are performative : believed widely enough, they reshape the world to fit themselves. The educated manager chooses the lens consciously . Key questions: What is the economy really about? Why do economists disagree? How do economic ideas shape management? Checkpoint (slide 4) — pas de corrigé “France raises the minimum wage by 10%. What happens to employment?” A: jobs disappear · B: demand and growth rise · C: almost nothing. (Vote and defend with one sentence.) The slides give no answer: each school would answer differently. 02 Partie 1 What is economics? No neutral definition “How you define it already smuggles in a worldview.” Definition Content Robbins (1932): scarcity Human behaviour as a relation between ends and scarce means with alternative uses . Mainstream view: the universal logic of allocation under rarity Aristotle: oikonomia vs chrematistikē Oikonomia = managing the household for a good life ( natural limit ). Chrematistikē = money-making for its own sake ( limitless ), judged unnatural. The 2,400-year-old question: is the economy for life, or life for the economy? What economics studies Classic circuit: production → exchange → distribution → consumption . How each step works and who gets what is where schools disagree. “Distribution” is where politics enters economics: who gets the value created is a choice, not a law . Hook: a firm is a small economy: it produces, exchanges and distributes value. Question de classe (pas de corrigé) A product is sold for €100. How should the value be distributed between employees, suppliers, shareholders, government, investment, communities, environment? The myth of neutrality Positive economics describes what is ; normative economics argues what ought to be . The line is real but porous: every model embeds values (what counts as welfare, whose preferences, what is “rational”). Performativity: taught widely, a model makes the world behave as it predicts — it helps produce the reality it claims to describe. Hook: adopting a metric quietly imposes the theory behind it on your whole organization. 03 Partie 2 The five schools (the map) “A timeline of arguments, not a museum. Each assumes a different human, market and state.” School Starts Key words Classical 1776→ invisible hand, free markets Marxist 1867→ value, exploitation, power Neoclassical 1870→ homo œconomicus, optimization Keynesian 1936→ demand, uncertainty, the state Critiques 1970→ behaviour, institutions, commons Classical Adam Smith , The Wealth of Nations (1776): division of labour (pin factory) multiplies productivity; self-interest led “as if by an invisible hand ” to benefit society; markets coordinate without a planner. Crucial nuance: Smith was a moral philosopher ( Theory of Moral Sentiments ) who grounded markets in sympathy and trust, not greed . Hook: specialization and competition still structure strategy but markets need morals to work. Ricardo — comparative advantage: even a country worse at everything gains by specializing where it is relatively best; the enduring case for free trade (still supports globalization and supply chains). Say — “Say’s Law”: production generates the income to buy it, so general gluts are impossible; he put the entrepreneur at the centre. Hook: “focus on your relative strength” is Ricardo; “build it and demand will come” is Say (and often dangerously wrong). Marxist Marx , Capital (1867): workers produce more value than their wage; the surplus value captured by capital is exploitation ; value comes from labour and its distribution is a relation of power . Whatever one’s politics, Marx forced distribution, conflict and power to the centre. Hook: “who captures the surplus along our value chain?” is a live strategic question. Neoclassical Marginal revolution (1870s): Jevons, Menger and Walras, independently, based value not on labour but on marginal utility ; economics rebuilt around the individual chooser. Foundation of every demand curve and pricing model. Hook: “price to the value of the next unit to the customer” is pure marginalism. Walras (general equilibrium: all markets clearing at once), Pareto (efficiency: no one better off without someone worse off), Marshall (toolkit: supply and demand, elasticity, the margin, short vs long run). Powerful but idealized; Pareto efficiency says nothing about fairness . Hook: every pricing analysis is Marshall’s scissors; beware “win-win”. Homo œconomicus: rational, self-interested, optimizing, stable preferences and (often) full information; social outcomes explained by aggregating such agents. Dominant in business schools and policy: elegant, tractable, “often wrong about real humans”. Hook: most optimization tools assume it. Hayek (Austrian turn) — the knowledge problem: no central planner can gather the dispersed, local knowledge that prices silently coordinate; the market is a spontaneous order. The deepest case for markets is information, not greed. Hook: over-centralized control destroys the local knowledge that prices and front-line teams hold. Friedman (Chicago): monetarism, faith in free markets, and the 1970 doctrine that “the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits.” Root of shareholder-value management; reshaped governance for fifty years, now fiercely contested. Hook: “maximize shareholder value” is one contested doctrine, not neutral common sense. Keynesian Keynes , The General Theory (1936): economies can get stuck in involuntary unemployment when aggregate demand is too low; under radical uncertainty investment swings on animal spirits ; the state can stabilize demand. Key terms: effective demand (spending drives output & jobs), animal spirits (confidence drives investment), the multiplier (one euro spent ripples outward). Hook: investment, hiring and M&A ride on confidence as much as on spreadsheets. Contemporary critiques Critique Idea Managerial hook Behavioral (Herbert Simon) Assault on homo œconomicus: bounded rationality (we “satisfice”); people are not rational optimizers but predictably irrational Design for the real humans you have, not the textbook ones Commons (Hardin → Ostrom) Hardin: shared resources are doomed (“tragedy of the commons”). Elinor Ostrom (first woman Nobel in economics) refuted the inevitability: communities govern commons successfully under identifiable design principles of governance Shared data, codebases, brand reputation and culture are commons: govern them by Ostrom’s principles Sen : capability approach Development = expansion of real freedoms : what people are actually able to do and be, not merely income or utility Measure what enables people to flourish, not only revenue Piketty : inequality returns When the return on capital exceeds growth (r > g), wealth concentrates structurally over time; inequality is a structural tendency Executive-pay ratios and wealth concentration are strategic reputational issues Raworth (2021): Doughnut Economy Social foundation (inner boundary: energy, equality, nutrition, decent work) and ecological ceiling (outer boundary: climate, biodiversity, deforestation, chemical pollution) A company cannot thrive for long in a world that is “failing” The school at a glance School Value comes from… Self-regulating

Idée centrale Determining cash flows is “the most important and difficult task in capital budgeting” . Only incremental, after-tax cash flows matter — not accounting profit. OCF = EBIT − Taxes + Depreciation and FCF = OCF − Capex − ΔNWC . 01 Révision The statement of cash flows Net income mixes accrual revenues and expenses, so it rarely equals the cash generated. The cash flow statement reclassifies every cash movement into three buckets: Bucket Content Meaning Operating (CFO) Collections from customers · payments to suppliers & employees · interest paid/received, taxes paid The engine of the business — day-to-day cash generation Investing (CFI) Purchases of PP&E / capex · sales of PP&E or land · purchases & sales of financial investments Building (or shrinking) the firm’s productive capacity Financing (CFF) New borrowings & loan repayments · share issuance & buybacks · dividends paid How the firm is funded — debt, equity, and payouts Direct vs indirect method — same answer, two routes Direct : lists actual cash receipts and payments (needs access to the cash account). Optional under IFRS / US GAAP, but firms using it must still disclose the indirect reconciliation. Indirect : starts from net income and adjusts for non-cash items — presented in the course as the mandatory presentation under IFRS & US GAAP. Indirect method CFO = Net income + Depreciation − Non-op. gains + Non-op. losses − ΔOperating assets + ΔOperating liabilities Exemple du cours (fictitious) — both methods give CFO = 93 Direct Indirect Collections from customers +1,191 Net income 55 Payments to suppliers −782 + Depreciation (non-cash) +54 Payments to employees −280 − Gain on land sale (non-operating) −4 Interest & taxes paid −36 − Δ Accounts receivable / inventory −15 CFO 93 + Δ Payables (A/P, interest payable) +3 CFO 93 Exemple du cours — Adobe Inc., FY2025 (10-K, $ millions) Item $M Net income 7,130 Depreciation & other non-cash items 2,296 Change in working capital 605 CFO 10,031 Capital expenditures −179 Acquisitions, net of investment sales/purchases −1,008 CFI −1,187 Share repurchases −11,281 Share issuance & net debt activity +845 Other financing activities −624 CFF −11,060 Cash bridge: beginning cash $7,613M + CFO 10,031 + CFI (−1,187) + CFF (−11,060) + FX effect 34 = ending cash $5,431M (net change −2,182). Despite $10.0B of operating cash flow, cash fell — driven by $11.3B of share repurchases, the largest use of cash. Free cash flow FY2025 = CFO 10,031 − Capex 179 = $9,852M . Capex is only ~2% of CFO in FY2025 vs ~5% in FY2021 (asset-light subscription software model). CFO up 39% since FY2021; CFF consistently negative (buybacks dominate). 02 Formules Operating cash flow & free cash flow OCF (project-level formula) \[ OCF = EBIT - Taxes + Depreciation \] Start from operating profit, remove cash taxes, add back the non-cash depreciation charge. FCF (firm-level formula) = Cash flow from assets \[ FCF = OCF - Capex - \Delta NWC \] Cash left after reinvesting in fixed assets and working capital — available to repay debt and reward shareholders. (In the notes: “change in net operating working capital”.) The same logic used to evaluate a single project scales up to a whole company. 03 Principes Project evaluation: which cash flows count? Definitions Project evaluation : applying one or more capital budgeting decision rules to the estimated relevant project cash flows to make the investment decision. Relevant cash flows : the incremental cash flows associated with the decision to invest in a project — any and all changes in the firm’s future cash flows that are a direct consequence of taking the project. Stand-alone principle : evaluating a project based on its incremental cash flows; view each project as a “mini-firm” with its own assets, revenues and costs. If projects interact, they can be bunched together. Issue Rule Only cash flow Estimate on an incremental basis (how the project changes the firm’s cash flows — especially relevant to depreciation); always after tax Sunk costs Do not include : past, irreversible outflows, not affected by the accept/reject decision Opportunity costs Include Side effects Include all incidental effects Net working capital Include : new projects often require cash, inventories and receivables; often recovered when the project ends Financing costs Not counted (interest, principal on debt, dividends): the discount rate takes care of them Key issues listed: when is a cash flow incremental · terminology: A. sunk costs, B. opportunity costs, C. side effects, D. net working capital, E. financing costs, F. other issues. Capital expenditure decisions listed: expand an existing product line · working capital · refunding · leasing · merger and acquisition · enter a new line of business · replacement · advertising campaign · R&D · education and training. 04 Méthode Specific rules for cash flow accounting 1. Initial outlay (−) Cost of the asset (installed) (−) Additional working capital investments (+) Cash flow from sale of an old asset (replacement situation): Selling price > book value: tax = (selling price − book value) × tax rate; CF = selling price − tax Selling price < book value: tax concession = (book value − selling price) × tax rate; CF = selling price + tax concession 2. Intermediate cash flows (operations) (+) Added revenues · (−) increased expenses, including overhead · (+) savings: labor and material (+) Depreciation expense (add back) Do not include interest expense. 3. Terminal cash flow (closing the business) (+) Sale of fixed assets (after the tax effect above) (+) Recapture of working capital Depreciation Straight line : a fixed percentage of the asset base. Modified ACRS (MACRS) : the 1986 Tax Reform Act allows firms to “front-load” depreciation charges. MACRS class Property 3-year Equipment used in research 5-year Autos, computers 7-year Most industrial equipment (furniture) 10-year Certain long-lived types of equipment 27.5-year Residential rental real property, including commercial and industrial buildings 31.5-year All non-residential real property, including commercial and industrial buildings Land cannot be depreciated. Contradiction dans les notes The 27.5-year class is described as “residential rental real property, including commercial and industrial buildings ”, and the 31.5-year class also lists commercial and industrial buildings. The notes do not resolve this; check with the professor before relying on it. 05 Exemple Norma Desmond Enterprises Exemple du cours — data Machine costs $21,000 , depreciated over 7 years straight-line . After 3 years, resale value expected $15,000 . Additional sales: 10,000 units/year at $5/unit. Variable cost $3/unit; fixed costs $5,000/year; project life 3 years. Investment in net working capital: $10,000. Required return (cost of capital) 20% ; tax rate 34% . Step 4 — Evaluation \[ NPV = -31{,}000 + \frac{10{,}920}{1.20} + \frac{10{,}920}{1.20^2} + \frac{34{,}900}{1.20^3} = 5{,}880 \] IRR = 29.5% > 20% → NPV > 0 and IRR > required return → the firm should invest (decision derived from the course rules; the notes leave the “Why or why not?” question open).
