sustainable-innovation/03-culture-leader: Question centrale How can an organization — whose habits, rules and success criteria were built around economic performance — be transformed so that it can design and develop more sustainable innovations? 01 Concept Organizational culture Definitions in the course Schein & Schein (2017): culture emerges from accumulated and shared learnings developed to solve problems of adaptation to the environment and internal integration . They define the appropriate way to perceive, think, feel and act. Chatman & O’Reilly (2016) / Delobbe & de Boer (2023): the set of norms that guides members’ attitudes and behaviours; it enables and channels social regulation and supports socialisation (especially of new arrivals). Schein’s 3 components Content 1. Visible artifacts and behaviours Practices, procedures, meetings, decisions, indicators, ways of operating 2. Espoused values What the company states is important: commitment, responsibility, innovation, sustainability 3. Fundamental assumptions Implicit beliefs, e.g. “The customer always chooses the cheapest option”; “Only financial results matter” Exemple du cours — Toyota “Continuous improvement and respect for people in everything we do.” The Toyota Way: learning organisation valuing mutual trust and long-term prosperity. Five principles: Respect, Challenge, Teamwork, Continuous improvement, Genchi Genbutsu (“go to the source”: verify the facts yourself to make a good decision). Exemple du cours — Decathlon “Focus on what you enjoy doing; you’ve got the right to try, to make mistakes and to try again.” Four values: Vitality (positive, full of energy), Responsibility (take charge of one’s life), Authenticity (true to oneself and others), Generosity (wholeheartedly, considerate of others). In a 2022 interview (slide 8, in French), Michel Leclercq says the two most important are Generous and Responsible , the most original in the capitalist system — “ce ‘et’ est important”. The slide on strengths and limits of an organizational culture (slide 9) asks the question without answer in the notes. Traditional organization focused on innovation Renewed organization focused on innovation Control and hierarchy · short-term performance · efficiency and cost reduction · workplace productivity · competition and dominance · trust · low-risk approach · blame · streamlining processes → inertia, incremental innovation Appropriateness and freedom to think differently · learning from mistakes · efficiency and value creation · instincts and actions · collaboration and sharing · experimentation · transparency and honesty · openness and agility → vision focused on change, radical innovation Point à vérifier On slide 10, “Trust” appears in the traditional column while “Transparency and honesty” is in the renewed one. This may be a slide placement error; the notes do not explain it. 02 Définition Culture focused on sustainability Principle Sustainability becomes a feature of culture when it influences values, beliefs, norms and day-to-day decisions , not merely the company’s stated commitments or environmental projects. Two definitions Linnenluecke & Griffiths (2010): a culture in which shared values and beliefs give sustainability a place within the organisation’s objectives and decisions. Assoratgoon & Kantabutra (2023): a set of fundamental assumptions, values and shared beliefs relating to the resolution of sustainability issues, which shape organisational behaviour through decisions and practices. Schein level Sustainability version (course adaptation) Fundamental assumptions The organisation regards itself as interdependent with society and the environment Values and norms Responsibility, cooperation and consideration of long-term impacts are legitimate decision criteria Artifacts and behaviours Eco-design, responsible procurement criteria, training, cooperation mechanisms, environmental and social indicators Piège : « green culture » ≠ sustainability culture A green organizational culture focuses only on the environment. Piwowar-Sulej (2020) offers a framework for a pro-environmental culture, distinct from the dimensions of sustainable development: environmental (preserve ecosystems and resources, limit pollution), social (needs, rights and well-being of people and stakeholders), economic (viability and long-term value creation). Four dimensions of a pro-sustainability culture (slide 13): 1. Politics & practices (importance given to the environment) · 2. Responsibility of sustainable resources (allocation of responsibilities, externalities) · 3. Communication & HR (measures for skills and awareness) · 4. Attitudes & behaviours (ownership in daily roles). Question sans réponse Slide 16: “List 6 dimensions that can be used to assess whether an organizational culture is conducive to sustainable innovation” — no answer given . The nearest material is the 4 dimensions above (not 6) and the 8 drivers below; do not treat either as the official list without checking. 03 Attention Greenwashing Greenwashing (eco-whitewashing): communication practices presenting a misleading environmental image of a company, product or service. It is not always an explicit lie: it may come from a “sincere” but poorly implemented policy. The DGCCRF distinguishes unfounded, misleading or disproportionate claims; a claim must be clear, verifiable and justified , and must not conceal significant life-cycle impacts. Mechanism Example (slide 14) Vague claim “Eco-friendly” without saying how or giving evidence Selective highlights Promoting a small green initiative as if it were the bulk of the business Overestimated benefits Presenting a limited emissions reduction as elimination of climate impact Promise not substantiated Future carbon-neutrality goal without means and assumptions Hidden impact transfer Highlighting recyclable packaging while ignoring impacts at other life-cycle stages Exemples du cours Volkswagen “clean diesel” : low-emission claims in the US while some vehicles had software to manipulate emission tests. FTC legal action March 2016; settlements June 2016 (buy-backs, compensation, funds to reduce pollution and support clean automotive technologies). KLM : sued by Fossielvrij over adverts, notably “Fly Responsibly”. On 20 March 2024 the Amsterdam court found several communications misleading and unlawful (too general claims; overly optimistic portrayal of alternative fuels and reforestation). KLM may still publicise initiatives if honest and concrete. 04 Cas + liste IKEA and the drivers of transformation Exemple du cours — IKEA (Elg & Welinder, 2022) IKEA develops circular business models (collection and resale of furniture, repairs, lifespan extension), adapting a business historically built on design, manufacture and sale of new furniture. → Contradictions between management strategy, product development and commercial practices: sustainable innovation requires transforming the whole value creation system . Transition underway: from selling new furniture to a system emphasising lifespan, repair, reuse and material recovery. Examples: sustainable-focused design (raw materials, manufacturing for recycling) · transformed supplier relations (long-term agreements) · training in-store sales staff for the recycling business · logistics decarbonisation · 2018: shared sustainability strategy across the franchise network · commitment to become “people and planet positive” by 2030. Drivers for more sustainable innovations (slide 18) Collectively redefine the criteria for sustainable innovation Embody transformation through exemplary leadership Align management and recognition systems Develop skills and supporting professional identities Encourage experimentation and challenging established routines Develop a culture of cooperation and open innovation Formalise long-term commitments with key partners, suppliers and stakeholders Embed the transformation in daily routines and collective learning Titre incohérent The slide title says “ 5 drivers” but lists 8 .
consumer-behavior-customer-experience-ma: Idée centrale We buy and consume many products because we want to highlight or hide some aspects of the self (feel successful, attractive, connect with a loved one). Consumers’ feelings about themselves shape their consumption practices — this is where Session 1’s symbolic consumption plugs into who we are (from symbolic to conspicuous consumption). Brands can turn this into customer experience through the self-image congruence model . 01 Concept Self-concept & self-esteem Self-concept The beliefs a person holds about his/her own attributes , and how he/she evaluates the self on these qualities. Dimension Meaning (slide) Content e.g. facial attractiveness vs mental aptitude Positivity self-esteem Intensity & stability over time Accuracy self-assessment vs reality Consumers’ self-assessments can be quite distorted , especially regarding physical appearance (slide example: “Snapchat dysmorphia”). The self is malleable We have as many selves as different social roles . Multiple selves: depending on the situation we behave differently, use different products and vary how we display ourselves. Role identities (dramaturgical perspective): only some are active at a given time (mother, worker, friend…); the dominant role shapes behaviour (dress, speech, attitude). Self-esteem The positivity of a person’s self-concept : the need to feel good about ourselves in our various roles. Self-concept theory: we have a concept of who we think we are ( actual / real self : realistic appraisal of the qualities we do and don’t have) and who we’d like to be ( ideal self ). The bigger the gap, the lower the self-esteem. → We buy products consistent with our actual self and products that help us reach an ideal standard . 02 Les autres Impression management & social comparison Impression management (Goffman, 1959) We work hard to “manage” what others think of us, presenting ourselves the way an actor performs for an audience . Theatrical metaphor: individuals select costumes, props and settings to project a desired identity. Front stage Back stage In public: plays a role and carefully manages their image In private: vigilance relaxes; behaves more naturally Slide images: a job interview and an Instagram grid (front stage); “Facebook version of you vs the realistic version” (back stage). Social comparison theory (Festinger, 1954) People evaluate their own appearance and worth by comparing themselves with others , especially in the absence of objective standards . Type Description Upward Comparing to someone better off: can motivate improvement — or spark envy and a sense of inadequacy Downward Comparing to someone less fortunate: often boosts self-esteem, sometimes at the cost of guilt Lateral Comparing to peers similar in status or skill: the most common everyday benchmark Self-esteem: constant exposure to high-achieving peers can lower mood and confidence. Motivation: healthy benchmarking can push consumers to study harder, train more, pursue goals. Digital behaviour: social media structurally favours upward comparison (users mostly post curated, idealised moments). 03 Numérique The digital self & new ways to express the self Digital environments let us construct multiple versions of the self . Form Content On social media LinkedIn (professional self), Instagram (aesthetic self), Facebook (social self): each platform stages a different version of you, anchored to your real-life identity As avatars Social media, gaming and VR let users assume virtual identities (realistic doubles to stylized, superhero-like characters). Consumers buy virtual goods (skins, outfits) to customize them Anti-consumption as self-defining Individuals may deliberately avoid certain products, practices or brands in order not to be associated with social groups their peers find undesirable. Avoiding can be as important as seeking. Boycotting or avoiding products can be a form of self-expression and emancipation . Slide image: “3 reasons to boycott Shein”. Embodied cognition Bodily states influence mental states. Physical experiences and interactions with products (wearing certain clothes, adopting particular postures, using a product) can shape how individuals perceive themselves and express their identity. Slide image: trail-running equipment. 04 Belk The extended self Extended self (Belk, 1988) The external objects, possessions, and even people or places that individuals consider part of themselves : belongings that help define one’s identity and self-concept. Roots — William James (1890): the Self is the sum of all we call ours (body, family, reputation, land, even money). Belk turned this into a testable marketing construct. Losing possessions = losing self: burglary and disaster victims often grieve like mourning a loved one (a bicycle-theft victim said the thief stole “a piece of my life”). Slide images: Nike By You (customized sneakers), Héloïse & Abélard (circular fine jewelry), football supporters. Level Content Slide example Individual Personal possessions Handbag, watch Family Residence and furnishings Redecorating a sideboard Community Neighbourhood or town you come from (sense of belonging) “Gavé bien Bordeaux” T-shirt Group Larger social groups, subcultures Punk band The extended self in a digital world (Belk, 2013) Dimension Meaning Slide note Dematerialization Music, photos and books become files, not objects Spotify Reembodiment We are not bodiless online: we become avatars Proteus effect: a taller avatar boosts real-world confidence Sharing Online disinhibition pushes self-disclosure past face-to-face norms Instagram Co-construction of self Others help build our identity in real time Comments add a “digital patina” to a photo Distributed memory Memory is outsourced, shared and searchable “On this day” photo memories 05 Composante 1 Personality Personality A person’s unique psychological makeup and how it consistently influences the way a person responds to his/her environment: a unique combination of inner characteristics ( traits ) that reflects individual differences and remains consistent and enduring over time . Marketers cannot change consumers’ personalities to meet their products, but understanding which traits drive the desired response helps them appeal to the target audience. Theory Era (slide) Core idea Psychoanalytic (Freud) 1900s Personality stems from unconscious conflicts Neo-Freudian 1930s–1950s Personality shaped by social relationships, not just instincts Trait theory 1940s–present Personality as a set of measurable, stable traits Freud & psychoanalytic theory Personality stems from a conflict between the desire to gratify physical needs ( Id , pleasure principle) and the need to function as a responsible member of society ( Superego , the person’s conscience). Component Principle Role Id (“ça”) Pleasure Immediate gratification, “party animal” of the mind, no regard for consequences Ego Reality Mediates between id and superego to find realistic solutions Superego Morality Counterweight to the id: conscience, internalizing society’s rules In consumer research: the Id points to unconscious motives guiding purchases; the Ego relies on symbolism in the product to reconcile them with the Superego’s constraints. Motivational research borrows these ideas to uncover deeper meanings behind products and ads (we channel socially unacceptable needs into acceptable outlets), mainly through depth interviews . Exemple du cours — motivational research “Acceptable” motive Associated products Unconscious motive Femininity (Baking) cakes and cookies Giving birth Masculinity Cars, red meat, shaving with a razor Expressing power, virility Social acceptance Sugar and honey Expressing love and affection Individuality Gourmet foods, cars, perfumes Showing how unique you are Neo-Freudian theories Social variables, not biological instincts , are the main force shaping personality (ongoing interdependence between individual and society). Jung — collective unconscious & archetypes Personality
sustainable-innovation/04-impact-assessm: Idée centrale Evaluating a sustainable innovation is not only showing that it yields environmental or social benefits. It also means measuring its impacts , identifying unintended / adverse side effects , and determining whether it genuinely contributes to transforming the system . 01 Distinction Output, outcome, impact Level Question Definition Example (clothing / repair) Output (deliverable) What did the organization produce, deploy or bring to market? What the organization produces, observable and measurable A new line of recyclable sweaters Outcome What changed for users or other stakeholders? Any change produced in beneficiaries / users / professional practices Consumer: proof the line is recyclable · subcontractors: must use dyes/raw materials allowing recycling · SMEs: a recycling market emerges Impact What difference does this make to society or the environment? Broader, systemic and lasting changes, positive or negative, to which the innovation contributes Lower resource consumption and emissions linked to product line turnover Social and environmental impact The totality of economic, social, environmental and cultural consequences that an activity or project generates for a community or society — positive or negative (e.g. job creation vs social exclusion or environmental damage). Course summary of social impact: aggregate of positive or negative, intended or unintended, lasting changes brought about by implemented activities and directly attributable to them ; environmental, economic or social in nature. Concerns external stakeholders (beneficiaries, users, direct/indirect clients) and internal ones (employees, volunteers), society and the environment. Concept introduced in the 1970s through academic research at Yale University on investors’ ethical responsibilities. Understood through an impact value chain : each link feeds the next; impact depends on context, actors, time horizons, and the ability to anticipate underserved needs through prevention, remediation or compensation. Exemple du cours — Solar lamp distribution Mission Strategy Action Output Outcome Impact Improve quality of life in developing countries Promote access to clean, affordable energy Sell solar lamps Number of lamps sold and people reached Better lighting, better economic standing, health, children’s education Economic improvement = reduction in energy spending minus what was caused by falling kerosene prices or household-size shifts (attribution / deadweight) 02 Cadre The 5 dimensions of impact # Dimension Content 1 Societal a) internally: working conditions and quality of relationships; b) externally: inclusive products/services for vulnerable or marginalised populations 2 Ecological Transition to eco-responsible practices and consumption; transformation of production, distribution, consumption models 3 Economic Wealth generation and equitable distribution of resources 4 Cultural Preservation and promotion of cultural heritage and collective identity 5 Governance Transparency, ethics and accountability in decision-making 03 Pourquoi Why evaluate? Three questions to measure impact effectively: What? (which outcomes, how important for stakeholders) · Who? (which populations, how underserved before) · How much? (how many people, depth/scale of change, how long it lasts). → evaluates breadth, depth and durability. Purpose: systematic risk prevention and active remediation of harms (social, environmental, human rights, governance) — with traceability and transparency . Evaluate to… Content Demonstrate Tangible evidence (monitor strategic execution) · verify the innovation delivers its sustainability promise · show value to all stakeholders → indicators tailored to each stakeholder group Act Correct or stabilise (organizational learning) · see which value-chain stages generate the most sustainability · systemic life-cycle approach · legitimise new behaviours (consumer “education”) Communicate Know how to let others know · tailor messages by stakeholder · protect credibility (avoid greenwashing) → be clear, accessible and transparent about impacts and methods Examples shown: Patagonia Worn Wear (repairs with guides and tutorial videos); Renault Flins Refactory. 04 Méthode How to measure: qualitative approach Measuring impact = determining what changes an innovation produces in the medium/long term, for whom , at what scale , and to what extent these changes can be attributed to it. Two approaches: qualitative and quantitative / monetized (SROI) . Qualitative approach (slide 14) Identify the 5 dimensions of impact; for each, rate its level/significance from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong) . Cas du cours (fil rouge) A non-profit provides low-cost electric cars + driving training to long-term-illness patients who are job seekers in underserved/isolated areas, so they can attend medical appointments. 100 patients, 1 year, €100,000. Information absente The slides do not give the 1-5 ratings for this case. A rating would be a judgement call; the correction was not provided. 05 Méthode SROI: the 6 steps SROI (Social Return on Investment) An accounting/evaluative method that measures and assigns monetary value to the social, environmental and economic value created by a project or investment, complementing traditional financial metrics . Establish scope and identify key stakeholders (internal and external). Key question: how do we engage those who are overlooked or rarely consulted? Map outcomes (clarify the change): impact map co-created with stakeholders, inputs → activities → outcomes; based on a theory of change / logic model. Evidence outcomes and give them value : indicators, data collection protocol (who, what, when), financial proxies . Establish impact : deadweight, attribution, displacement, drop-off. Calculate the SROI : future projections → NPV → ratio → sensitivity analysis → (optional) payback period. Report, use and embed . Step 4 — the deductions Concept Meaning Slide example Deadweight Part of the outcome that would have happened anyway , without the intervention; needs a baseline benchmark Natural exit rate from unemployment benefits for long-term job seekers in the same region (vs a vocational programme) Attribution Share of the outcome due to others’ contributions (other organisations/interventions) Solar lamps: change not due to falling kerosene prices Displacement How much the outcome simply displaced other positive outcomes or shifted a problem elsewhere Street lighting cuts crime in one area, adjacent precincts see crime rise; ex-offender jobs that would have been filled by other job seekers Drop-off Decline of the outcome’s value over time (applied to later years) 20% per year in the case Net impact, year 1 \[ \text{Gross value} = \text{Quantity} \times \text{Proxy} \] \[ \text{Year 1 net} = \text{Gross value} \times (1-\text{deadweight}) \times (1-\text{attribution}) \times (1-\text{displacement}) \] Later years: apply the drop-off each year (year 2 = year 1 × (1 − drop-off)). Present value, NPV, SROI ratio \[ PV = \sum_{t} \frac{\text{net impact}_t}{(1+r)^t} \qquad NPV = PV - \text{Investment} \qquad SROI = \frac{PV}{\text{Investment}} \] Here \(r\) = discount rate (3.5% in the course case). The ratio is read as “€X of social value for every €1 invested”. 06 Exemple complet The electric-car case (course data) Step 1 — stakeholders (slide 16) Patients · caregivers/family · healthcare professionals/facilities · health insurers/mutuals/public authorities · local/territorial authorities · the non-profit association. Step 3 — outcomes and proxies (slides 18-19, “pedagogical assumptions”) Stakeholder Outcome / indicator Proxy Quantity, duration Patients Maintained health (drop/stabilisation in prescription drug use; CPAM data) €1,000 / patient / year 60 patients, 2 years Patients Keeping medical appointments (records from doctors, clinics, hospitals) €500 / patient / year 80 patients, 2 years Caregivers Reduced burnout (CPAM data); quality-of-life survey as a complem

Exercice du cours — refaire le calcul Electric cars for patients — SROI Investment €100,000. Outcomes (pedagogical assumptions): patients’ health 60 × €1,000 (deadweight 20%, attribution 20%, 2 yrs) · appointments 80 × €500 (15%, 10%, 2 yrs) · caregivers 50 × €600 (25%, 20%, 2 yrs) · facilities 120 × €100 (10%, 10%, 1 yr). Displacement 0% everywhere; drop-off 20% per year; discount rate 3.5%. Compute the SROI. Voir la correction 1. Year-1 net = gross × (1 − deadweight) × (1 − attribution): 60,000 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 38,400 · 40,000 × 0.85 × 0.9 = 30,600 · 30,000 × 0.75 × 0.8 = 18,000 · 12,000 × 0.9 × 0.9 = 9,720 → 96,720 (corrigé du cours) . 2. Year 2 (drop-off 20%; facilities last 1 year only): 38,400 × 0.8 + 30,600 × 0.8 + 18,000 × 0.8 = 30,720 + 24,480 + 14,400 = 69,600 . 3. Discounting at 3.5% : 96,720 / 1.035 = 93,449 ; 69,600 / 1.035² = 64,968 (slide; exact value 64,972) → PV = 158,417 . 4. NPV = 158,417 − 100,000 = 58,417 . SROI = 158,417 / 100,000 = 1.58 : 1 . 5. Interpretation: each €1 invested generates about €1.58 of discounted social value (pedagogical scenario). Payback (calculé, optional step of the course): after year 1 cumulated PV = 93,449 < 100,000; remaining 6,551 on year 2’s 64,968 → payback ≈ 1 + 6,551 / 64,968 ≈ 1.10 years (using the course’s simple formula “time for cumulative discounted benefits to match the investment”, assuming benefits spread evenly across year 2). Questions de la séance sans corrigé Qualitative approach (slide 14): rate the 5 dimensions of impact from 1 to 5 for the same case. No answer is given in the course documents : do it as an exercise, but there is no official correction to check against. Exercices d’entraînement Exercice d’entraînement généré A — Output, outcome or impact? Classify: (1) a repair service completes 2,000 repairs; (2) customers keep their garments longer and buy fewer new ones; (3) a lasting reduction of resource consumption and emissions linked to product turnover. Voir la correction (1) Output : what the organization produces, observable and measurable. (2) Outcome : change for users (behaviour). (3) Impact : broader, lasting change for society/environment (this wording follows the clothing example of the course). Exercice d’entraînement généré B — Which deduction? Name the SROI deduction: (a) a training programme claims all job placements, but the region’s natural exit rate from unemployment is high; (b) a lighting scheme cuts crime locally while neighbouring areas see more crime; (c) other organisations also support the same people on the same outcome; (d) the value of an outcome falls each year after the programme. Voir la correction (a) Deadweight (would have happened anyway; baseline = natural exit rate). (b) Displacement . (c) Attribution . (d) Drop-off . Exercice d’entraînement généré C — Full SROI calculation A programme costs €50,000. sociology-social-transformations-managem: Idée centrale There is no view from nowhere. Every claim about truth, the good and the just comes from a worldview. Philosophy lets you name which one and choose . Every managerial act assumes one: name it, and judge by it. 01 Introduction Why philosophy for managers Where we left off: Session 3 revealed that every economic school conceals a vision of the human being and the good life. Today: from each discipline’s assumptions down to their philosophical roots (“philosophy is where the assumptions are”). Opening — the 5 “whys” Take an “obvious” management truth (a good manager is rational and data-driven · the customer is always right · competition makes us better). Keep asking “why?” like a four-year-old (or Socrates). Within 4 or 5 whys, the obvious dissolves into a value choice . That dissolving is philosophy: not abstraction but the discipline of seeing the assumptions you stand on . 3 reasons it matters Every decision rests on unexamined assumptions about truth, the good and the just. Surface them and you decide better. The hardest problems aren’t technical but philosophical: what is fair? what do we owe people? what is the point? Philosophy gives the markers to situate any idea (“markers, not slogans”). Key questions (the spine): What is truth? (epistemology, knowledge & reality) · What is a good life? (ethics: virtue, joy, meaning) · What is a just decision? (moral & political philosophy). 02 Partie 1 What is philosophy? “The love of wisdom”: the disciplined activity of questioning foundations. Socrates — the founding gesture Invented the method: relentless questioning that exposes how uncertain our “knowledge” is. Stance: “ I know that I know nothing ” — wisdom begins in acknowledged ignorance. Tools: irony and maieutics (helping others give birth to their own ideas). Philosophy is not answers but a practice of examination. Hook: the best strategic question is often the naïve one: “why do we actually do it this way?” Domain Questions Metaphysics What is real? What exists? Epistemology What is truth? What can we know? How do we know it? Ethics What is a good life? What is good, virtuous, worth living for? Political What is a just decision? How should we live together? Use it: most meetings stall by confusing a question of facts (epistemology) with a question of values (ethics). Beyond doxa: philosophy distrusts doxa (opinion, the “self-evident”) and demands reasoned argument. “Everyone knows that…” is where philosophy starts. The goal is not cynicism but clarity : holding beliefs you have examined. Hook: reasoned doubt is not indecision, it is the prerequisite of a decision you can defend.
